title: The Estrada enigma
primary_topics: Estrada-disqualification doctrinal column June 30, 2013 -- first of two-part Estrada arc (A454 June 30 → A453 July 7)

Estrada Manila mayoralty victory; Comelec proclamation; Alfredo Lim conceded; takes oath at noon today -- however 'legal challenge earlier dismissed by Comelec may have gained some traction due to very recent en banc jurisprudence, Comelec v. Jalosjos'

Brief-background: Sept 12, 2007 Sandiganbayan sensational trial 2001-2007 conviction of plunder + reclusion perpetua (~life imprisonment) + accessory penalties civil interdiction during sentence + perpetual absolute disqualification

Forfeitures: (1) P545M 'with interest and income earned... deposited in name and account of Erap Muslim Youth Foundation' (2) P189M 'inclusive of interest and income earned, deposited in Jose Velarde account' (3) 'Boracay Mansion' in Quezon City

262-page decision by Sandiganbayan special division: Presiding Justice Teresita Leonardo-De Castro (now SC) + Justice Francisco Villaruz Jr. (later PJ, now retired) + Justice Diosdado Peralta (now SC); Estrada denounced as 'kangaroo court'; Saguisag: 'The special division was programmed to convict. We never had a chance'

GMA's pardon Oct 25, 2007 (Acting ES Ignacio R. Bunye co-signed); Oct 26 walked free after 6.5 years detention; verbatim pardon-text three clauses: (1) WHEREAS 'publicly committed to no longer seek any elective position or office' (2) 'I hereby grant executive clemency... He is hereby restored to his civil and political rights' (3) 'forfeitures... remain in force and in full... including all writs and processes... except for bank account(s) he owned before his tenure as President'

Petitioners Alicia Risos-Vidal + Alfredo Lim (joined two weeks ago) argue: pardon based on 'no longer seek any elective position' commitment, did not restore right to run for elective office; Sandiganbayan's 'perpetual absolute disqualification' not expressly erased by pardon
Favoring Estrada: 'emphatic provision' restoring 'his civil and political rights' (right to vote/be voted is political right); 'by his election to office, people are deemed to have pardoned him'

Convoluting-enigma: Jalosjos v. Comelec ruled 'accessory penalty of disqualification remains even though one is pardoned as to principal penalty unless accessory penalty shall have been so expressly remitted in the pardon'; perpetual/temporary absolute disqualification 'carr(y) with (them) the deprivation of the right to vote in any election for any popular office or to be elected to such office'; presumption 'one who is rendered infamous by conviction of a felony or other base offense indicative of moral turpitude, is unfit to hold public office'

Three distinctions: (1) Estrada plunder vs Jalosjos 2 counts statutory rape + 6 acts of lasciviousness (both reclusion perpetua) (2) Estrada executive clemency vs Jalosjos presidential commutation after 6 years (3) Estrada voted to office vs Jalosjos not voted (name not printed on ballot by Comelec); 'Will these distinctions make a difference? Abangan!'
sub_topics: Former president Joseph Ejercito Estrada won mayoralty race in Manila
Commission on Elections proclaimed him winner, opponent Alfredo Lim publicly conceded victory
In fact, he will take his oath and assume office this noon
However, legal challenge earlier dismissed by Comelec may have gained some traction
Due to very recent en banc jurisprudence, Comelec v. Jalosjos
Recall that on Sept 12, 2007, Sandiganbayan -- after sensational trial from 2001 to 2007 -- found him guilty of plunder
Sentenced him 'to suffer penalty of reclusion perpetua (roughly equivalent to life imprisonment)'
And accessory penalties of civil interdiction during period of sentence and perpetual absolute disqualification
Moreover, it forfeited in favor of government:
(1) P545 million 'with interest and income earned... deposited in name and account of Erap Muslim Youth Foundation'
(2) P189 million 'inclusive of interest and income earned, deposited in Jose Velarde account'
(3) so-called 'Boracay Mansion' in Quezon City
Verdict was handed down by special division of antigraft court composed of:
Then Presiding Justice Teresita J. Leonardo de Castro (now member of Supreme Court), who wrote 262-page decision
Justice Francisco H. Villaruz Jr. (later became presiding justice, now retired)
And Justice Diosdado M. Peralta (now also member of Supreme Court)
Estrada denounced Sandiganbayan as 'kangaroo court'
His counsel, Rene A.V. Saguisag, blurted, 'The special division was programmed to convict. We never had a chance'
Despite criticisms and initial attempts to appeal his conviction to Supreme Court
Former President ultimately accepted decision and penalties when he scribbled his agreement to executive clemency
Granted him on Oct 25, 2007 by then President GMA
Next day, Oct 26, he walked free after being detained for six and a half years
For clarity's sake, let CJP copy verbatim pertinent portion of 'pardon' signed by President Arroyo and Acting Executive Secretary Ignacio R. Bunye:
'WHEREAS, Joseph Ejercito Estrada has publicly committed to no longer seek any elective position or office'

'IN VIEW THEREOF and pursuant to authority conferred upon me by Constitution, I hereby grant executive clemency to JOSEPH EJERCITO ESTRADA, convicted by Sandiganbayan of Plunder and imposed penalty of Reclusion Perpetua'
'He is hereby restored to his civil and political rights'

'Forfeitures imposed by Sandiganbayan remain in force and in full, including all writs and processes issued by Sandiganbayan in pursuance hereof, except for bank account(s) he owned before his tenure as President'
In asking Supreme Court to unseat him, petitioner Alicia Risos-Vidal, later joined by Lim two weeks ago, argued:
By its clear wording, presidential pardon was based on Estrada's commitment 'to no longer seek any elective position or office'
Hence, pardon did not restore his right to run for any elective office
Furthermore, Sandiganbayan's imposition of accessory penalty of 'perpetual absolute disqualification' from holding public office was not expressly erased by pardon
Favoring Estrada, on other hand, is emphatic provision of presidential pardon restoring 'his civil and political rights'
Certainly, right to vote and to be voted is political right
Moreover, by his election to office, people are deemed to have pardoned him
Convoluting Estrada's legal enigma is Jalosjos v. Comelec, which ruled:
'Accessory penalty of disqualification remains even though one is pardoned as to principal penalty'
'Unless accessory penalty shall have been so expressly remitted in pardon'
(This decision, as of CJP's deadline, is not yet posted in Supreme Court website
Neither could Court's spokesman, Prof. Theodore Te, give CJP copy
CJP took preceding quotes from June 19 Rappler report)

Supreme Court held 'that penalties of perpetual or temporary absolute disqualification carr(y) with (them) deprivation of right to vote in any election for any popular office or to be elected to such office'
It further explained: 'This is based on presumption that one who is rendered infamous by conviction of felony or other base offense indicative of moral turpitude'
'Is unfit to hold public office, as same partakes of nature of privilege which State grants only to such classes of persons (who) are most likely to exercise it for common good'
Big question is whether Court will apply this ruling to unseat Estrada, considering:

(1) He was convicted of plunder while Romeo Jalosjos was found guilty of two counts of statutory rape (capital offense for which he, like Estrada, was imposed reclusion perpetua) and six counts of acts of lasciviousness
(2) He was granted executive clemency while Jalosjos was given only presidential commutation (reduction) of sentence, after serving six years of original penalty
(3) He was voted to office while Jalosjos was not because his name was not printed on ballot by Comelec
Will these distinctions make a difference? Abangan!

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the first installment of his two-part Estrada-Manila-mayor arc, the doctrinal half (the personal-encounter follow-up comes next week in A453), filed on the very day of Erap's noon oath-taking. Former president Joseph Ejercito Estrada won the mayoralty race in Manila -- the Comelec proclaimed him the winner, and his opponent, Alfredo Lim, publicly conceded his victory; in fact, he will take his oath and assume office this noon; however, a legal challenge earlier dismissed by the Comelec may have gained some traction due to a very recent en banc jurisprudence, Comelec v. Jalosjos. Brief background: recall that on Sept 12, 2007, the Sandiganbayan -- after a sensational trial from 2001 to 2007 -- found him guilty of plunder and sentenced him 'to suffer the penalty of reclusion perpetua (roughly equivalent to life imprisonment) and the accessory penalties of civil interdiction during the period of sentence and perpetual absolute disqualification.' Moreover, it forfeited in favor of the government (1) P545 million 'with interest and income earned... deposited in the name and account of the Erap Muslim Youth Foundation,' (2) P189 million 'inclusive of interest and income earned, deposited in the Jose Velarde account,' and (3) the so-called 'Boracay Mansion' in Quezon City. The verdict was handed down by a special division of the antigraft court composed of then PJ Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro (now a member of the SC), who wrote the 262-page decision, Justice Francisco H. Villaruz Jr. (later became presiding justice, now retired), and Justice Diosdado M. Peralta (now also a member of the SC); Estrada denounced the Sandiganbayan as a 'kangaroo court,' and his counsel, Rene A.V. Saguisag, blurted, 'The special division was programmed to convict. We never had a chance.' GMA's pardon: despite these criticisms and initial attempts to appeal his conviction to the SC, the former President ultimately accepted the decision and the penalties imposed on him when he scribbled his agreement to the executive clemency granted him on Oct 25, 2007 by then President GMA; on the next day, Oct 26, he walked free after being detained for six and a half years. For clarity's sake, let CJ copy verbatim the pertinent portion of the 'pardon' signed by President Arroyo and Acting Executive Secretary Ignacio R. Bunye: 'WHEREAS, Joseph Ejercito Estrada has publicly committed to no longer seek any elective position or office, IN VIEW THEREOF and pursuant to the authority conferred upon me by the Constitution, I hereby grant executive clemency to JOSEPH EJERCITO ESTRADA, convicted by the Sandiganbayan of Plunder and imposed a penalty of Reclusion Perpetua. He is hereby restored to his civil and political rights. The forfeitures imposed by the Sandiganbayan remain in force and in full, including all writs and processes issued by the Sandiganbayan in pursuance hereof, except for the bank account(s) he owned before his tenure as President.' In asking the SC to unseat him, petitioner Alicia Risos-Vidal, later joined by Lim two weeks ago, argued that by its clear wording, the presidential pardon was based on Estrada's commitment 'to no longer seek any elective position or office' -- hence, the pardon did not restore his right to run for any elective office; furthermore, the Sandiganbayan's imposition of the accessory penalty of 'perpetual absolute disqualification' from holding public office was not expressly erased by the pardon. Favoring Estrada, on the other hand, is the emphatic provision of the presidential pardon restoring 'his civil and political rights' -- certainly, the right to vote and to be voted is a political right; moreover, by his election to office, the people are deemed to have pardoned him. Warped enigma: convoluting Estrada's legal enigma is Jalosjos v. Comelec, which ruled that 'the accessory penalty of disqualification remains even though one is pardoned as to the principal penalty unless the accessory penalty shall have been so expressly remitted in the pardon.' (This decision, as of CJ's deadline for this column, is not yet posted in the SC website; neither could the Court's spokesman, Prof. Theodore Te, give CJ a copy; CJ took the preceding quotes, as well as those below, from a June 19 Rappler report.) The SC held 'that the penalties of perpetual or temporary absolute disqualification carr(y) with (them) the deprivation of the right to vote in any election for any popular office or to be elected to such office.' It further explained, 'This is based on the presumption that one who is rendered infamous by conviction of a felony or other base offense indicative of moral turpitude, is unfit to hold public office, as the same partakes of the nature of a privilege which the State grants only to such classes of persons (who) are most likely to exercise it for the common good.' The big question is whether the Court will apply this ruling to unseat Estrada, considering (1) that he was convicted of plunder while Romeo Jalosjos was found guilty of two counts of statutory rape (a capital offense for which he, like Estrada, was imposed reclusion perpetua) and six counts of acts of lasciviousness, (2) that he was granted executive clemency while Jalosjos was given only a presidential commutation (or reduction) of sentence, after serving six years of the original penalty, and (3) that he was voted to office while Jalosjos was not because his name was not printed on the ballot by the Comelec -- will these distinctions make a difference? Abangan!
